story.hook: My Neighbor Towed My Car From My Own Spot
story.script: I got home from work one evening and found an empty space where my car was supposed to be. At first I thought I had parked on the wrong floor, but the painted number on the ground was mine and the little parking permit sign was still bolted to the wall. I called building security, and the guard told me a tow truck had removed my car less than an hour earlier after another resident reported that I was using a reserved space without permission. That made no sense because the space was written directly into my lease. I asked who had made the complaint. Security would not give me a name, but they said the resident had shown the tow driver a photo of a handwritten notice that supposedly warned me to stop parking there. I had never seen any notice. I called the towing company. They confirmed they had my car and told me I could collect it after paying the tow fee and overnight storage. I explained that the space was mine, but the dispatcher said their driver had been told I was blocking another resident's assigned parking and that the building had authorized the removal. Instead of arguing on the phone, I asked them to email me the tow authorization and the photographs their driver took before moving the car. They sent everything within ten minutes. The first photo showed my car sitting perfectly inside the numbered space. The second showed a sheet of paper taped to my windshield saying I had been warned repeatedly. The third photo was much more useful. It included the wall beside my car, where my unit number and parking permit were clearly visible. I forwarded the photos to the building manager with my lease page showing the same parking number. She replied almost immediately and asked me not to pay the tow company yet. Then she checked the security desk log. Twenty minutes later she called me back sounding annoyed. The building had never authorized the tow. A resident from the next floor had approached the driver directly and claimed the space belonged to him. He had apparently been parking there whenever I was away because it was closer to the elevator. When I started working from the office again and used my space every day, he decided I was the problem. The manager pulled the garage camera footage. It showed him walking up to my car that afternoon, placing the handwritten warning under my wiper, taking a picture of it, and removing it again. About fifteen minutes later, the tow truck arrived. The footage also showed him pointing to my space while talking to the driver. The manager called the towing company herself. Once they saw my lease and learned that no authorized building representative had requested the tow, their attitude changed very quickly. They brought my car back that night at no charge and apologized for accepting the complaint without verifying it. I thought that was the end of it until the next morning, when an email went out to the entire building reminding residents that only management could authorize towing from assigned spaces. It also said anyone making a false towing report would be responsible for the resulting charges and could lose parking privileges. Later that day I saw the neighbor at the elevator. He asked why I had made such a big deal about a simple misunderstanding. I told him I had not reported him at all. I had only asked for my car back. He looked relieved for about three seconds. Then the building manager stepped out of the office and handed him an envelope. Because the towing company had already dispatched a truck, processed the vehicle, and returned it, they had billed the building for the wasted service call. Management passed that charge directly to the person who made the unauthorized request. The next week, his vehicle was no longer in the convenient space near the elevator. Management had moved his assigned parking to the far end of the garage for the rest of his lease term. He tried to get my car removed from my own parking spot. In the end, my car came back for free, and he was the one who lost the good spot.
